q: Flexible couplings: state the basic function, and how the motor is aligned to its load.
a: Joins the motor shaft to the load shaft end to end, so both turn together
Absorbs shock, vibration and small misalignment (and allows for shaft expansion)
Align with a straight edge first, then check with a feeler gauge at 4 points 90° apart — all four gaps equal = aligned

q: State the TWO basic functions of a flexible coupling.
a: Transmits power (torque) from one shaft to the other so both rotate together at the same speed
Compensates for small misalignment, movement and vibration between the two shafts

q: Two flanges directly couple a motor to its machine. Describe (with sketches) two types of misalignment and how to minimise them.
a: Angular misalignment: the gap is wider on one side than the other (X ≠ Y)
Parallel (offset) misalignment: the shaft centres are offset by a distance P
Minimise both to within the manufacturer's tolerances (shim the feet, re-check with feeler gauge / dial gauge)

q: Describe how to remove a worn bearing and fit a new one on a motor shaft.
a: Remove with a bearing puller — do not bend or damage the shaft
Heating the bearing (not the shaft) helps it come off
Fit the new one with a press and sleeve pushing on the INNER race only
Make sure it is the right way round

q: Where are thermistors located in the overcurrent protection of a 3-phase induction motor?
a: Embedded in the motor windings
Wired to a thermistor control relay that opens the control circuit when the windings get too hot

q: Name two methods of coupling a motor to drive a load.
a: Solid (direct) coupling
Flexible coupling
Vee-belt drive
Flat belt drive

q: (a) How must AC cables entering a ferromagnetic enclosure be arranged? (b) PVC/PVC cable without armour buried in a solid wall: the 3 permitted methods?
a: (a) All conductors of the circuit, including the CPC, in the same enclosure — only collectively surrounded by steel, never one per hole
(b) Within 150 mm of the room edges, or a straight horizontal/vertical run to the point or accessory
(b) Protected against harmful substances in plaster/concrete (PVC conduit or suitable sheath)
(b) Not less than 50 mm from the reverse side of the wall

q: (a) Which types of cable are recognised by CENELEC? (b) Colour code for multicore cables and cords on AC circuits?
a: (a) Harmonised cables — carry the <HAR> mark plus the approval body (e.g. BASEC, VDE)
(a) Approved national types — marked on the sheath
(b) Line: brown (L1), black (L2), grey (L3)
(b) Blue = neutral (or mid-point) only
(b) Green/yellow = protective conductor only

q: (a) Flexible cables and cords — requirement regarding mechanical damage? (b) Separated circuits — what about their exposed-conductive-parts?
a: (a) Must be visible along any part of their length liable to mechanical damage
(b) Must NOT be connected to the protective conductor, to exposed parts of other circuits, or to earth

q: State two methods of connecting luminaires to the fixed wiring.
a: A box (to I.S. EN 60670)
A DCL outlet — Device for Connecting a Luminaire (I.S. EN 61995)
Equipment designed to be connected directly to the wiring system

q: Describe the construction of STP cable used in Cat6 structured cabling.
a: 4 pairs of insulated copper conductors
Each pair twisted, each with a different twist rate
Foil/metal shield around the pairs (that is the "S" in STP)
Overall outer jacket

q: Describe the construction of UTP cable used in Cat5e structured cabling.
a: 4 pairs of insulated copper conductors
Each pair twisted, with different twist rates
NO shield (unshielded)
Overall outer jacket

q: Describe three ways low-voltage and extra-low-voltage (Band I & II) circuits can share a wiring system.
a: Every cable insulated for the highest voltage present
Each core of a multicore insulated for the highest voltage in it
Separate compartment of trunking/ducting
Cable tray with a partition between them
Separate conduit or trunking system

q: Underground communication cables cross or run close to power cables: minimum clearance, and the alternatives?
a: Keep at least 100 mm apart
OR a fire-retardant partition between them (bricks, clay/concrete cable covers, shaped blocks, fire-retardant conduit or troughs)
OR at crossings, mechanical protection between them (conduit, concrete caps or blocks)

q: Where must "Solar PV on roof" warning signs be placed?
a: At the origin of the installation
At the metering position, if it is away from the origin
At the consumer unit / distribution board the inverter is connected to

q: Compare aluminium to copper: mechanical properties, cost, current-carrying capacity, conductivity.
a: Weight: aluminium is about 3 × lighter — easier to handle, used for big and overhead cables
Cost: aluminium is cheaper, and its price is more stable
Conductivity: aluminium is only about 61 % of copper
So it needs a bigger size for the same current (about one size up, e.g. 25 mm² Al ≈ 16 mm² Cu)
r: Min Al size for power/lighting: check ET101 Table 52

q: PVC/PVC cable in a wall cavity likely to touch expanded polystyrene: what must be done?
a: Do not let PVC stay in contact with expanded polystyrene (it draws out the plasticiser — PVC goes brittle)
Run it in conduit or another enclosure that polystyrene will not attack

q: Installing aluminium cable for power circuits: the requirement for the connectors?
a: Connectors used to terminate aluminium conductors must be tested and approved for that specific use

q: Recommended minimum bending radius for a cable with an aluminium sheath?
a: D = the overall (outer) diameter of the cable (unless the manufacturer says otherwise)

q: (a) What determines the current-carrying capacity of a cable? (b) List four factors to consider.
a: (a) Must not exceed the value from the Annex 52 tables, after correction factors are applied
(b) Ambient temperature
(b) Method of installation
(b) Grouping with other circuits
(b) Thermal insulation · load current · volt drop · fault loop impedance

q: How can data cabling be protected from electromagnetic interference (EMI)? Two methods.
a: Use shielded (STP/screened) cable
Keep it separated from power cables — e.g. multi-compartment trunking
Earthed steel trunking around unshielded cable near sources of interference

q: Cable I²R losses: state three ways to reduce them.
a: Reduce the volt drop in the wiring
Increase the conductor cross-sectional area
Fit power factor correction
Reduce harmonic currents

q: State three factors that affect I²R power losses in a cable.
a: Cable length
Conductor cross-sectional area
The load current

q: 10 mm² cable, 40 m run, 38 A, 4.4 mV/A/m. Volt drop? Is it OK?
a: Limit is 4 % of 230 V = 9.2 V → it complies
Practise more of these in the Formula Lab

q: Describe the electrolytic effect between copper and aluminium, and how to prevent it.
a: Moisture at an Al–Cu joint acts as an electrolyte → the aluminium corrodes quickly
Use bi-metallic (Al/Cu) lugs or connectors
Coat the joint with anti-oxidant paste/grease
Tin-plated Al lugs only in rooms that stay dry

q: What does ET101 require when connecting dissimilar metals liable to cause electrolytic action?
a: They must not be placed in contact unless special arrangements are made to avoid the effects of the contact
(Quote the rule — the examiner wants the regulation, not just "use a bi-metal lug")

q: State four precautions when connecting aluminium cables into copper busbars.
a: Isolate — busbar and cable dead
Connection clean and dry (keep moisture off)
Use a bi-metallic lug, with contact grease inside
Tighten to the correct torque

q: With a diagram, explain discrimination between protective devices.
a: Devices are chosen so the one nearest the fault (on the supply side) operates first
Fault on a final circuit: only that circuit's fuse/MCB goes
Sub-board and main fuse stay in, so the rest of the building keeps power
Diagram: Supply → main fuse → sub-board fuse → final circuit fuse → fault X

q: An RCD is marked 32A / 30mA / AC. Explain each part.
a: 32 A — rated current it can carry continuously
30 mA — residual (earth leakage) current that trips it
AC — type: for loads with no significant DC component

q: Why must T-568A and T-568B terminations not be mixed in one installation?
a: The green and orange pairs swap pin positions between the two
Mixed ends → pairs do not line up at plugs and jacks → data signals will not transfer
Pick one (usually T-568B in Europe) and stay consistent — mixed ends only for crossover leads

q: A wall-mounted DB has its bottom less than 1.4 m from the floor. What is required, and why?
a: It must be accessible only to responsible persons (e.g. lockable)
Reason: to stop young children getting at it

q: Draw the internal connections of a 3-phase DB: 3-phase heater, 3-phase motor, 4 lighting circuits, 2 socket circuits.
a: Main switch / fuse-switch feeding L1, L2, L3 busbars + neutral bar + earth bar
3-phase loads: triple-pole (TP) MCB taking L1, L2 and L3
Single-phase loads spread across L1, L2, L3 to balance the phases
Sockets on RCBOs (RCD protection)
Every circuit clearly labelled, neutrals to N bar, CPCs to E bar

q: Complete the DB drawing: heating (3-phase), lighting 1, lighting 2, printing machine — protected by fuses.
a: Heating: a fuse in each of L1, L2, L3 (triple-pole)
Lighting 1, lighting 2 and the printing machine on different phases (balance)
Each single-phase fuse fed from its busbar; neutrals to N bar
Label every load

q: On an MCB tripping curve, identify the maximum and minimum tripping curve regions.
a: Minimum curve = the left/lower edge of the band (to the left it will not trip)
Maximum curve = the right/upper edge (to the right it will always trip)
Upper curved part = thermal (overload), the drop = magnetic (short circuit)

q: Why are MCBs backed up by HBC fuses in industrial installations? What does HBC mean?
a: MCBs have a limited breaking (rupturing) capacity — may not clear very high fault currents
HBC = High Breaking Capacity

q: Explain the purpose of an HBC fuse and draw its construction.
a: Safely breaks very high fault currents; good discrimination; used as back-up
Ceramic body
Silver element (with notches/necks)
Quartz sand filler to quench the arc
Brass end caps and fixing tags · indicator

q: Which MCB/RCBO type for circuits with very high inrush current? What range of magnetic tripping can it ignore?
a: Type B: trips at 3–5 × In — general/resistive loads
Type C: 5–10 × In — inductive loads (fluorescent lighting, small motors)
Type D: 10–20 × In — VERY high inrush (transformers, welders, big motors)

q: Short-circuit faults at A (near supply), B and C (far end). Where is the fault current lowest, and why?
a: Lowest at C — the point furthest from the supply transformer
The further out the circuit, the higher the impedance → less fault current

q: Steel conduit, 8 m run, 2 bends: 2 × 2.5 mm² circuits and 3 × 1.5 mm² circuits (stranded single-core). Conduit is the CPC. Cable factors and minimum conduit size?
a: Conduit is the CPC → only L + N per circuit (2 cables each)
2.5 mm²: 4 cables × 30 = 120
1.5 mm²: 6 cables × 22 = 132
Total 252 → 25 mm conduit (factor 292) is enough
r: ET101 Tables 52J.3 & 52J.4 — your model answers are not consistent on this, check with the tutor

q: (a) Bell wires (ELV) inside a DB: precaution? (b) Diagram: mounting heights for switches, sockets and DB.
a: (a) Sleeve ELV cables to the highest voltage in the board, or keep them physically separated
(b) Switches in dwellings: 400–1200 mm (public buildings 900–1200 mm)
(b) Sockets: 400–1200 mm above finished floor
(b) DB: top not more than 2.25 m; bottom not less than 1.4 m

q: Domestic DB: mounting height rules (with diagram) + four places it cannot go.
a: Readily accessible; top ≤ 2.25 m, bottom ≥ 1.4 m
Not in a storage or airing cupboard
Not under timber stairs
Not in a bathroom, washroom or WC
Not above a cooker/heater, or where clothes could cover it

q: Four exemptions from mechanical protection for cables in hollow walls (partitions)?
a: Within 150 mm (horizontally) of a room corner
Within 150 mm (vertically) of the ceiling
Straight horizontal or vertical run directly to an accessory, appliance or DB
At least 50 mm from the reverse side of the wall

q: Describe three precautions when installing a rising main busbar system.
a: Seal every floor penetration to the fire resistance of that floor (and fit internal fire barriers in the trunking)
Correct IP rating — no water or dust ingress; seal floors against water leaking between levels
Expansion joints in tall runs; adequate supports at the maker's spacing
Mechanical protection where needed

q: Six advantages of a rising main busbar system over cables in a multi-storey building.
a: Strong over long runs with few fixings → faster to install
Replaces many cable runs and their supports
Easier to handle than lots of large cables
Less termination space in switchboards; no lugs except at the feeder
Takes up less space; bends and offsets fit tight areas
Type-tested fault ratings · lower volt drop · better fire resistance · can be reused

q: Where water or high humidity may occur, what three requirements must the installer consider?
a: No damage from condensation or water — IP rating suitable for the location
Provide a way for collected water/condensation to escape
Where waves may hit it, protect it against mechanical damage

q: Non-armoured cable in a pipe in the ground (industrial/commercial): type of pipe, and minimum depth?
a: Pipe: high-density polythene, high-impact PVC, or spigotted concrete
Depth: your model answers differ — 450 mm (2021, 2024 papers) and 250 mm (2023 paper D). Check ET101 522.8 and ask the tutor which he wants

q: Cable suitable for burying in a domestic garden, and minimum depth?
a: SWA (steel wire armoured)
At least 450 mm (600 mm where the ground is likely to be dug, from your Q&A notes)

q: Cable between two buildings, in the soil: precautions required?
a: Protect against mechanical damage OR bury deep enough to minimise the risk
Mark buried cables with cable covers or marking tape
Buried conduits and ducts must be identified

q: Drawing cables into an underground duct: one advantage, one disadvantage.
a: Advantage: repairs and additions from manholes without digging; cable need not be armoured; well protected
Disadvantage: higher initial cost; poorer heat dissipation → lower current rating

q: Pulling large cables into a duct with rollers and jacks: three precautions.
a: Jacks and rollers rated for the drum weight and width
Jacks on level ground, axle level
Rollers placed so the cable is not strained or damaged
Cable comes off the bottom of the drum so it cannot tip; use pulling lubricant on long runs with bends

q: Why are expansion joints fitted on long busbar runs? What fault if they are not?
a: Busbars expand and contract with the heat from load current
Without joints the bars can warp → clearances to other bars/the case reduce
Constant movement loosens joints → high-resistance hot joints

q: (a) Overhead busbar trunking vs fixed wiring: one advantage, one disadvantage. (b) Minimum size of supplementary bonding conductor with underfloor busbar trunking?
a: (a) Advantage: machines plugged in/out (tap-off units) without shutting down the rest
(a) Disadvantage: expensive to install at first
(b) 2.5 mm² copper where mechanically protected
(b) 4 mm² copper where NOT mechanically protected

q: Underfloor / raised-floor power-track: one advantage, one disadvantage.
a: Advantage: flexible when the floor layout is unknown; 13 A / 32 A tap-offs; modular floor boxes; clean-earth versions
Disadvantage: usually only up to 63 A; limited tap-offs; runs about 20 m max; proprietary parts can be hard to get

q: ET101 requirements for busbar trunking and powertrack systems?
a: Busbar trunking to I.S. EN 60439-2; powertrack to I.S. EN 61534
Selected and installed to the manufacturer's instructions, allowing for external influences

q: Give two reasons multi-compartment trunking is popular in commercial buildings.
a: Keeps circuits of different voltage bands segregated (power, data, telecoms)
One neat run instead of several unsightly runs
Fast and easy to install

q: Ten cells, 1.5 V each, 0.2 Ω internal resistance each, series, 4 Ω load. Current? + two recharging methods.
a: Recharging: constant current
Constant voltage

q: Testing lead-acid batteries for a large diesel generator: equipment, procedure and PPE.
a: PPE: goggles, rubber gloves, heavy apron · ventilated room · no naked flames
Fully charge, disconnect, inspect; note voltage on a voltmeter
Load tester across terminals for 15 s — should stay above about 9.5 V (12 V battery)
Let it recover ~30 s, repeat; still above 9.5 V = good

q: VRLA (valve-regulated lead-acid) batteries: three handling precautions, and the charging method.
a: Sealed, but the gel/paste inside is still corrosive if the case cracks — handle carefully, do not drop
Wear apron, gloves and goggles
Charging: constant voltage

q: Compare lead-acid and Ni-Cad batteries: weight, applications, charging method, cost.
a: Weight: lead-acid heavy; Ni-Cad about 50–60 % lighter
Uses: lead-acid in cars, trucks, forklifts, UPS · Ni-Cad in medical devices, power tools, aircraft
Charging: lead-acid constant voltage (heat must be managed) · Ni-Cad constant current, tolerates abuse
Cost: lead-acid cheap, 3–10 yrs · Ni-Cad dearer but lasts 25+ yrs

q: A hydrometer checks a lead-acid battery. What does it test, and the reading when fully charged?
a: The specific gravity (density) of the electrolyte
Fully charged: about 1.25–1.28

q: Self-contained emergency lighting: describe two of the three quarterly test requirements.
a: Simulate mains failure via the test facility: at least 30 min (3 h units) or 10 min (1 h units), max ¼ of rated duration — check every luminaire lights
Afterwards, check every charging/status LED shows healthy
Issue a report to the owner and put a copy in the logbook

q: Central battery vs self-contained emergency lighting: four comparisons.
a: Battery life: central up to ~25 yrs · self-contained batteries replaced periodically
Install cost: central high · self-contained low (needs local unswitched supply)
Testing: central from one place · self-contained each fitting tested
Failure: central battery fault kills the whole system · self-contained fault affects one fitting

q: Self-contained emergency luminaire: four main components.
a: Battery
Charger
Control unit
Lamp(s) / LEDs
Diffuser / cover · test facility

q: Describe the tests and procedures for emergency lights and exit signs.
a: Quarterly: run each light on battery for 30 minutes
Annual: run on battery for the full 3 hours
Examine fittings for condition and function
Fill in the logbook and issue a test certificate

q: Briefly describe how a central battery emergency lighting system works.
a: One central battery, kept charged by its charger and control gear
Feeds many luminaires (AC or DC)
Supplies them when the mains fails, or all the time if maintained

q: Define a "Combined (Sustained) Emergency Luminaire".
a: Contains at least two lamps
One fed from the normal lighting supply, the other from the emergency supply
Gives light at all material times

q: List three factors escape lighting must provide to comply with the Irish Standard.
a: Clearly show the escape routes
Light at each change of direction
Light at each change of level
Enough light along routes to move safely to and through the exits

q: Describe four areas where emergency lighting units should be installed.
a: At each exit door and outside each final exit
Near each staircase (each flight lit)
Near any change of floor level
Near fire-fighting equipment and fire alarm call points
Lift cars · toilets (incl. disabled) · plant, switch and control rooms

q: Define an emergency lighting luminaire.
a: A luminaire used for safety or emergency lighting
It may or may not have its own power source for safety services

q: Maintained, non-maintained and combined luminaires: the difference?
a: Maintained: lamp on all the time (mains or battery)
Non-maintained: lamp only lights when mains fails
Combined: two or more lamps, at least one on the emergency supply

q: Compare SOX (low-pressure sodium) and MBF (high-pressure mercury): colour rendering, efficacy, run-up time.
a: Colour rendering: SOX poor · MBF reasonable
Efficacy: SOX about 180 lm/W · MBF about 50 lm/W
Run-up: SOX about 10 min · MBF about 4 min

q: Compare CFL and HID lamps: colour rendering, efficacy, run-up time.
a: Colour rendering: CFL reasonable–good · HID good
Efficacy: CFL about 50–70 lm/W · HID about 40–100 lm/W
Run-up: CFL full output at switch-on · HID about 15 s to 5 min

q: Compare fluorescent and LED lamps: colour rendering, efficacy, run-up time.
a: Colour rendering: fluorescent reasonable–good · LED reasonable–very good
Efficacy: fluorescent about 30–70 lm/W · LED about 100–200 lm/W
Run-up: both give full output when switched on

q: Describe the high-pressure mercury (MBF) lamp from switch-on to full light.
a: Arc strikes first between the starting electrode and a main electrode
Gas ionises, the tube warms, then the arc strikes between the main electrodes
Heat vaporises the mercury → light and pressure rise
Phosphor on the outer bulb turns UV into visible light; takes several minutes

q: Why are MBI (metal halide) lamps suited to high-bay industrial, high-mast and stadium lighting (incl. colour TV)?
a: Good colour rendering (white light)
Good efficacy
Available in high wattages

q: Describe four factors that affect lamp life.
a: Operating voltage and voltage spikes
How often it is switched on/off or dimmed
Ambient temperature
Mechanical shock · lamp orientation · manufacturing defects

q: SOX lamps: one place they suit, one place they do not.
a: Suitable: car parks, roads (colour does not matter)
Not suitable: paint spray booths, shops, loading bays — poor colour rendering

q: (a) Define luminous flux and its SI unit. (b) 5 m × 7 m floor receives 10,500 lumens. Average illuminance?
a: (a) The total light given out by a source — measured in lumens (lm)

q: (a) Define illuminance and its unit. (b) Room 7 m × 12 m at 400 lux: total luminous flux?
a: (a) Luminous flux falling on a surface per square metre — lux (lm/m²)

q: What meter measures the lighting level in a room, and what is it measuring?
a: A lux meter
It measures illuminance (E) in lux

q: Lighting control strategy for offices with good daylight: describe four types of control.
a: Dimmable (or on/off) luminaires throughout
Automatic switching: PIR / presence sensors switch off when nobody is there
Daylight-linked photo-electric sensors dim lights near windows
Local manual switches close to each work area (within about 6 m)
Time-controlled switching, or a central lighting/building management system (wired or wireless)

q: Office 8 m × 14 m needs 400 lux. Lamps 3600 lm, UF 0.7, MF 0.85. (a) Total flux? (b) Number of luminaires? (c) Controls?
a: (c) Dimmable fittings, PIR sensors, daylight photo-cells, central control system

q: (a) What stores the heat in a night storage heater — and what precaution when mounting? (b) Draw the internal wiring: 3 elements, thermal cut-out, charge controller.
a: (a) High-density clay/ceramic blocks — very heavy
(a) Fix securely to a wall and floor strong enough for the weight
(b) L → thermal cut-out → charge controller (input thermostat) → 3 elements in parallel → N

q: Describe a fan-assisted night storage heater, with its circuit.
a: Elements charge the blocks on the restricted (off-peak) supply
A fan boosts heat output during the day
The fan is on the unrestricted (24 h) supply, via spur or socket — NOT the off-peak supply
Fan controlled by a room thermostat, switch or time clock

q: What device controls the charge (input) of a storage heater, and how does it work?
a: The charge controller (input / auto-charge control)
A dial sets a bi-metal thermostat that limits how hot the core gets → how much heat is stored overnight

q: What does the damper on a storage heater do?
a: A flap that controls air flow through the blocks
Controls how much heat comes out during the day

q: How does the supply authority control and monitor a storage heating system?
a: A separate circuit just for the storage heaters
Controlled by a sealed time switch — supply only in off-peak hours
Measured on a separate off-peak meter

q: Underfloor flexible heating mats under tiles: four installation requirements.
a: Subfloor flat, with no screws or nails sticking up
Insulation under the heated area
Thermostat/controller outside the room, with a floor probe between the heating cables
RCD / RCBO protection

q: (a) Construction of an electric radiant flexible sheet/mat. (b) Installation precautions.
a: (a) Heating cable fixed to a fibreglass mesh or foil; rolls ~500 mm wide; 100–200 W/m²; cannot be cut shorter
(b) Never cut, cross or overlap the heating cable
(b) Not under fixed furniture (baths, units); keep 100 mm from pipework
(b) RCD protection; floor sensor between the cables; limit foot traffic until the floor is down

q: Name two systems used in off-peak underfloor electric heating.
a: Withdrawable systems — silicone rubber or fibreglass cables in conduit
Mineral-insulated cables embedded directly in the screed
PVC-insulated cables embedded directly in the screed

q: Two precautions when installing embedded floor-warming cables.
a: Screed well compacted — voids cause hot spots
Cables must not cross or touch; keep the spacing
Do not lay PVC cable below about 4 °C (goes brittle)
Never cut or coil surplus cable — adjust the last spacings instead

q: Why do some mechanical thermostats need a neutral? The advantage?
a: To feed a small "accelerator" heater inside the thermostat
It warms the bi-metal slightly while calling for heat, so it switches off a little early
Advantage: closer, more even room temperature (less overshoot)

q: Compare S-Plan and Y-Plan systems: operation, valves and controls.
a: S-Plan: a separate 2-port spring-return zone valve for each zone (heating + hot water)
S-Plan: room stat for each heating zone, cylinder stat for hot water, 2-channel programmer
Y-Plan: one 3-port mid-position valve shares the flow between heating and hot water
Y-Plan: room stat + cylinder stat + programmer; valve can sit mid-position to feed both

q: In an S-Plan Plus system, explain how the 2-port valves control hot water and the heating zones.
a: Used when there are several heating zones plus a hot water zone
Each zone has its own 2-port spring-return valve and its own room stat
Cylinder stat controls the hot water temperature
Zones and hot water controlled separately by a 2-channel programmable time clock

q: Identify this system (one 3-port mid-position valve) and describe how it works.
a: Y-Plan
Boiler and pump controlled by a programmer, room stat and cylinder stat
The mid-position valve sends flow to heating, hot water, or both
Fully pumped system

q: Purpose of main protective bonding, and minimum size in a domestic installation?
a: Connects extraneous-conductive parts (water, gas, oil pipes, structural steel) to the main earthing terminal
Keeps metalwork at the same potential during a fault → reduces shock risk
Minimum 10 mm² in a domestic installation (from your Q&A notes)

q: Earthing requirement for equipment marked with the double-square symbol?
a: It is Class II (double insulated)
Do NOT connect an earth to it

q: List any five tests to verify an installation complies with the ETCI rules.
a: Visual inspection
Continuity of protective conductors
Insulation resistance
Polarity
Earth fault loop impedance
Operation of RCDs

q: Which ET101 test, used with insulation resistance, finds faulty connections between circuits before the supply is connected?
a: Detection of erroneous connections between circuits
Switch off each circuit, disconnect loads, and insulation-test between its line conductors and all other line conductors

q: How does a shaded-pole motor make a rotating field?
a: Part of each pole has a copper shading ring
Current induced in the ring delays the flux in that part
Flux sweeps from the unshaded part to the shaded part
This moving field drags the cage rotor round — fixed direction

q: Why do motors use laminated cores?
a: Thin insulated steel sheets
Break up eddy current paths
Less heat, less iron loss, better efficiency

q: What is no-volt protection and how is it done?
a: Stops a motor restarting by itself when power returns after a loss
Done by the contactor: when voltage drops, the coil drops out
The hold-in (retaining) contact opens — Start must be pressed again

q: Two reasons for rotor-resistance starters on large motors?
a: Lower starting current
High starting torque (max torque at start when R₂ = X₂)
Some speed control

q: Star vs delta: voltage and current rules?
a: Star: V<sub>L</sub> = √3 × V<sub>ph</sub>, I<sub>L</sub> = I<sub>ph</sub>
Delta: V<sub>L</sub> = V<sub>ph</sub>, I<sub>L</sub> = √3 × I<sub>ph</sub>
P = √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ for both

q: Two conditions for maximum current in a series RLC circuit?
a: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub> (resonance)
So Z = R (minimum impedance)
Power factor = 1, current in phase with voltage

q: Sketch hysteresis loops for high-loss and low-loss material.
a: High loss: wide, fat loop (hard steel — permanent magnets)
Low loss: narrow, thin loop (silicon steel — transformer cores)
Area of loop = energy lost each cycle

q: What is ripple voltage? Single-phase vs 3-phase?
a: The leftover AC "wobble" on the DC output of a rectifier
Single-phase full-wave: big ripple (2 peaks per cycle)
3-phase full-wave: much less ripple (6 peaks per cycle)

q: Linear power supply: one advantage, one disadvantage?
a: Advantage: simple, very clean low-noise output
Disadvantage: heavy transformer, inefficient — wastes energy as heat

q: Oscilloscope: what do the X and Y axes show? What do the Y-plates do?
a: X axis: time (time/div)
Y axis: voltage (volts/div)
Y-plates deflect the beam up and down in proportion to the input voltage
